selected.title: RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' as next decision looms
selected.summary: As markets put the chance of a rate hike in November at 42 per cent, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser warns of a "central banker's nightmare".
selected.why: Hawkish central bank warning signaling worsening inflation and potential rate hike.
selected.fullText: RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' ahead of November meeting - ABC News Skip to main content Skip to news navigation, settings and search Explore the ABC news iview listen Loading ABC News News Home RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' ahead of November meeting Share Share article RBA deputy warns inflation outlook 'materially worse' ahead of November meeting By business reporter Stephanie Chalmers Topic: Interest Rates Posted Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 12:01pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 12:01pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 12:01pm , updated Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 3:46pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 3:46pm Wed 21 Oct 2026 at 3:46pm Andrew Hauser warns the inflation outlook has become more grim. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) In short: The RBA deputy governor says there are signs some people do not expect inflation to come back to the RBA's target, which is "central banker's nightmare". Markets are putting the chance of a November rate hike at more than 50 per cent. What's next? The RBA's rate-setting board will next meet at the beginning of November, with a decision handed down on Melbourne Cup day. abc.net.au/news/reserve-bank-hauser-warns-inflation-outlook-materially-worse/107288574 Link copied Share Share article Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser says the inflation outlook is "materially worse" than the RBA had forecast, raising the prospect of another interest rate hike as soon as November. Just under a fortnight out from the next interest rate decision, Mr Hauser warned high inflation was becoming entrenched in the Australian economy. "We are beginning to see some signs that some people in the community are not sure if we're going to bring inflation back into target at all, or certainly not for an extended period," Mr Hauser told the Citi Investment Conference in Sydney. The RBA targets headline inflation between 2 and 3 per cent on average over time. Inflation currently sits at 4 per cent, according to the August consumer price index . Mr Hauser said the central bank's liaison program and surveys showed there was "an increasing share of businesses who are thinking that, maybe, sort of 3 per cent, 3.5 per cent [inflation] is the new normal". "Look, that is the central banker's nightmare. "We can't allow expectations to shift away from target." reason: RBA inflation warning creates genuine debate: does entrenched inflation justify rate hikes despite employment cost, or should the bank tolerate higher inflation to avoid recession?
angle: Central banks facing de-anchored inflation expectations should raise rates aggressively now rather than wait, even if it costs jobs immediately.
